overall_summary: Analysis of the deduplicated performance data reveals that extreme cosmic anomalies and high-stakes 'What If' space scenarios are heavily dominating viewer retention, engagement velocity (likes-per-view), and daily views. Videos addressing extreme planetary physics and surreal environments (e.g., liquid diamond planets, burning ice, and extreme dark worlds) outperform standard biological or psychological facts by a significant margin. Engagement is concentrated in formats leveraging curiosity-inducing questions and visual impossibility hooks.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (IYuce8vaU3Y) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (8KEl0_pJ_68) achieved the highest modern velocity, recording over 970 to 1,029 views and strong like ratios (up to 38 likes) despite being published weeks prior.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on hypothetical space disaster/immersion scenarios involving extreme, visually arresting environments.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing extreme planetary phenomena such as 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' (A9Qa-RmuOr0) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (QXuqYERlqSo) generated high view counts (725-981 views) and high comment/like ratios.
winning_patterns.action: Produce more micro-documentaries centered on terrifying or impossible weather and time anomalies on newly discovered exoplanets.

weak_patterns.evidence: Content focusing on psychological tricks, memory manipulation, or songs stuck in the head (e.g., ef3ND4qiRHc, Jc04LVKNd2s, 2fqaGqfsR4A) consistently stalled between 5 to 71 views with near-zero engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize standalone psychological facts unless paired with a high-concept sensory mystery or a dramatic narrative.

weak_patterns.evidence: Simple animal biology facts like 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' (AXAfwrzzEdU) saw diminishing returns on repeated iterations compared to fresh space or physics concepts.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid standard textbook biological trivia; shift animal content strictly into cinematic survival or extreme evolutionary adaptations.

next_video.concept: A rogue planet completely stripped of its star, wandering interstellar space while burning at 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit from internal radioactive decay.
next_video.opening_direction: Start with total darkness and absolute cold, then instantly reveal a glowing, molten world hurtling through the void with no sun in sight.
next_video.twist_direction: Explain that because it has no star, its atmosphere rains literal glowing rock while the surface acts as an infinite, hyper-dense nuclear reactor.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven high-performing 'What If / Extreme Planet' framework while introducing a completely fresh exoplanet archetype (rogue nuclear-heated worlds) that avoids previous duplication.
fresh_topic_constraints: Must not mention diamonds, glass, iron, rubies, or standard water ice weather.
Must focus entirely on an untethered rogue astronomical body.

experiment: Test a 21-second narrative structure that opens on a sensory paradox ('This planet has no sun, yet it melts steel') to measure retention drop-off compared to standard question-based hooks.
